pdf_title: PDF Speed Reader, Free Online, No Upload | Speeedy
pdf_description: Open a PDF and speed read it word by word or with a guided highlight. The file never leaves your device. Free, no account, works offline.
pdf_lead: Open a PDF and read it one word at a time. The file is read in your browser and never uploaded.
pdf_opens_text: A PDF that holds text opens: the kind where you can select and copy words in a PDF viewer. Speeedy reads the text in page order, one column after the other when a page has columns.
pdf_opens_furniture: Page numbers, and headers or footers that repeat from page to page, are left out so they do not cut into a sentence.
pdf_opens_hyphens: Most words split by a hyphen at the end of a line are joined back together.
pdf_opens_images: Images are not read, only text.
pdf_scan_text: A scan is a set of pictures of pages, with no text in it. Speeedy checks for this and stops with a message: “This PDF is a scan: it holds pictures of pages, not text. Paste the text instead.” Speeedy does not do OCR (text recognition).
pdf_scan_todo: What to do: run the file through an OCR tool, which turns the pictures into text, then open the result here. If you already have the text somewhere else, paste it into the box above.
pdf_locked_text: A PDF locked with a password, or otherwise protected, does not open. Speeedy does not remove locks, so use a copy without one.
pdf_limits_text: Files up to 100 MB open. If reading a PDF takes more than 3 minutes, Speeedy stops and says so.
pdf_course_text: If your readings come as PDFs, open one here and read it at a pace you choose. If you lose the thread, go back a sentence or a paragraph.
epub_title: EPUB Speed Reader, Free in Your Browser | Speeedy
epub_description: Open a DRM-free EPUB and read it with RSVP, Pacer or Listen, picking up where you left off. Free, no account, the book stays on your device.
epub_lead: Open an EPUB and read it one word at a time. The book stays on your device.
epub_opens_text: An EPUB without DRM opens. Speeedy reads the book in the order the book sets, and each chapter heading becomes a stop you can jump to.
epub_opens_skipped: Covers, pictures, style sheets and fonts are skipped. Pages a book marks as optional, such as a cover or a footnote page, are left out too.
epub_opens_jump: Use the chapter list or the progress bar to move around the book.
epub_drm_text: A book with DRM (copy protection) does not open. Speeedy says: “This book is protected by DRM (copy protection), so Speeedy cannot open it. Use a copy of the book without DRM.” Speeedy does not remove DRM.
epub_place_title: Picking up where you left off.
epub_place_text: Speeedy keeps each book you open in your Library, on this device, with your place in it. Open the same book later and it carries on from there.
epub_place_private: The Library stays in your browser, and nothing you read is uploaded.
epub_other_text: Kindle files (MOBI, AZW and AZW3) do not open yet. Speeedy says so and asks you to paste the text instead. Files up to 100 MB open.
adhd_title: ADHD Reading Tool: One Word at a Time | Speeedy
adhd_description: Read one word at a time in a fixed spot, at a steady pace. A small 2025 study found this helped students with ADHD at about 200 WPM. Free, no account.
adhd_headline: One word at a time, at a steady pace.
adhd_lead: Each word appears in the same spot, so your eyes do not move along a line. The reader starts at 220 words per minute, and you can change that at any time.
adhd_preset_note: Start opens the reader with the focus preset: 220 WPM.
adhd_study_text: Moussaoui, Siddiqi, Cheung and Niemeier (2025) tested 38 undergraduates with ADHD and 38 without. Each read passages three ways: as a normal paragraph, with words appearing one at a time in their normal place, and with one word at a time in a single spot (RSVP) at 250 milliseconds a word plus a 50 millisecond gap. That is about 200 words per minute.
adhd_study_result: Readers with ADHD scored about 7% better with RSVP than in the two conditions where the eyes move. Readers without ADHD scored about 6% worse, a trend that was not statistically significant. The difference between the two groups, about 13%, was significant.
adhd_study_pacing: Showing words at the same pace but in their normal place made no difference for either group. So the benefit appears to come from the fixed spot, not from the pacing alone.
adhd_limits_title: What the study cannot tell you.
adhd_limit_size: It is one small study, the first of its kind. The authors call it an “initial step”.
adhd_limit_online: It ran online, with no eye tracking, so nobody measured whether eyes stayed still.
adhd_limit_items: Each reader saw only seven passages per condition, with one question each, and the study did not run a power analysis.
adhd_limit_recruit: The group with ADHD did better overall, a sign of recruitment bias.
adhd_limit_scope: It tested young adults at one speed. It does not tell us how this works for children, for other ages or at other speeds.
adhd_limit_you: Results are group averages. They do not say it will help you.
adhd_limit_ours: The study did not use Speeedy, so its result is not a measurement of this tool. Speeedy is a reading tool, not a treatment or medical advice.
adhd_preset_text: The study ran at about 200 words per minute. This page opens the reader at 220 words per minute instead. That is Speeedy's own choice within a range of 200 to 250, not a result of the study. Set the speed to 200 if you want to match the study.
adhd_tweak_text: You can change the speed at any time while you read. Each sentence end is held a little longer by default. If you lose your place, go back a sentence or a paragraph.
tts_title: Free Text to Speech Reader with Word Highlight | Speeedy
tts_description: Hear your text read aloud while each word lights up as it's spoken. The built-in voice runs on your device, offline, after a one-time 31 MB download.
tts_headline: Text to speech that follows along.
tts_lead: Listen reads your text aloud and marks where it is. Paste text or open a file, then switch to Listen in the reader.
tts_device_body: Speeedy's own voice is a model that runs in your browser. It speaks English. The voice model is 31 MB, and with its voice file and pronunciation lists the whole one-time download is 37 MB. Nothing downloads until you choose to start it.
tts_device_offline: Once it is on your device it works offline, and your text never leaves your device. If the download is interrupted, it can carry on from where it stopped.
tts_device_timing: The model reports when each word starts and ends, so the highlighted word is the word you hear.
tts_device_slow: If your device is too slow to keep up, Speeedy measures that and switches to a browser voice.
tts_browser_body: Browser voices are the fallback. They work at once with no download, and use the voices your browser and system already have. Listen highlights the sentence being spoken. Words inside a sentence are only estimated unless your browser reports them, so do not count on the exact word being lit.
tts_cache_title: What is kept on your device.
tts_cache_body: Audio Speeedy makes is kept on your device, so a repeat does not have to be made again. The audio caches share 500 MB, and the oldest audio is dropped first.

home_learn: What the research says about speed reading
learn_refs_access_abstract: Only the abstract and highlights were read.
learn_refs_access_review: The full text was not read. The 2016 review by Rayner and colleagues summarises it.
learn_hub_title: Learn: Reading Speed, Backed by Research | Speeedy
learn_hub_description: Three short articles: how to read faster, what RSVP is, and average reading speed. Each claim names the research it comes from.
learn_hub_headline: What speed reading can and can't do.
learn_hub_lead: Three short articles. Each claim carries a number that leads to the paper behind it, listed at the end of the article.
learn_faster_title: How to Read Faster: What the Research Says | Speeedy
learn_faster_description: Read faster without losing the meaning? What the main research review concluded, what has evidence behind it and what does not.
learn_faster_lead: This article sets out what the research supports about reading faster, and what it does not. Each claim has a numbered source at the end.
learn_faster_summary: What the main review concluded about speed and understanding, and what has research behind it.
learn_faster_tradeoff_review: Rayner, Schotter, Masson, Potter and Treiman (2016) reviewed the research on how we read and whether speed reading helps. They concluded that readers are “unlikely” to double or triple their speed, from about 250 to 500–750 words per minute, and still understand the text as well. Speed and accuracy trade off.
learn_faster_tradeoff_skill: The review's answer to reading faster with good understanding is to become a more skilled language user. In its words, “Language skill is at the heart of reading speed.”
learn_faster_lookback_title: Looking back is part of reading.
learn_faster_lookback_mask: Schotter, Tran and Rayner (2014) had 40 students read sentences in which each word turned into Xs once their eyes left it, so a word could not be seen again. This works like the lack of look-back in RSVP, which shows one word at a time. Comprehension dropped for both ambiguous and unambiguous sentences.
learn_faster_lookback_repair: In normal reading, readers looked back mostly when they had failed to understand something. Looking back is a repair move, not a bad habit. The authors explicitly question speed-reading apps that remove eye movements.
learn_faster_lookback_rewind: Speeedy lets you go back a sentence or a paragraph while you read.
learn_faster_training_pressure: Breznitz and colleagues (2013) trained typical and dyslexic adults to read under time limits that were set for each person and tightened over sessions. Speed and comprehension both improved, and the gains held at 6 months. The same training without time pressure did not work.
learn_faster_training_modest: Training methods in general, the 2016 review argues, give at most modest gains unless they build language skill.
learn_faster_skimming_cost: A classic comparison by Masson (1983), which the 2016 review summarises, found that both skimming and RSVP raise speed at the cost of comprehension. So treat very high speeds as skimming, not as reading faster for free.
learn_faster_skimming_rsvp: RSVP, the one-word-at-a-time style many speed readers use, has its own article.
learn_faster_bionic_snell: Bionic Reading bolds the start of each word. Snell (2024) had readers read 100 paragraphs in Bionic or normal type and found no significant difference in reading time.
learn_faster_bionic_parker: Parker, Wang, Lee and Joseph (2026) ran a pre-registered eye-tracking study of 90 skilled adult readers. Bolding the start of a word pulled the first fixation toward the start of long words, but there was no change in skipping, word reading times, sentence reading times or comprehension.
learn_rsvp_title: What Is RSVP Reading? Evidence and Limits | Speeedy
learn_rsvp_description: RSVP shows text one word at a time in one spot. What the research says about it, from the main review's caveat to a small study with ADHD readers.
learn_rsvp_lead: RSVP stands for rapid serial visual presentation. It shows text one word at a time in the same spot on screen. This article sets out what the research says about it.
learn_rsvp_summary: One word at a time in one spot: where it holds up, where it costs understanding, and what it cannot promise.
learn_rsvp_caveat_review: The main review of the field, by Rayner, Schotter, Masson, Potter and Treiman (2016), concluded that readers are “unlikely” to double or triple their speed, from about 250 to 500–750 words per minute, and still understand the text as well.
learn_rsvp_caveat_skill: The review's own summary of what limits reading speed is this: “Language skill is at the heart of reading speed.”
learn_rsvp_removes_lookback: RSVP removes look-backs by design: each word is gone when the next one appears. Schotter, Tran and Rayner (2014) tested something close to this, with a mask that turned each word into Xs once the eyes left it, and comprehension dropped (40 students).
learn_rsvp_removes_more: Why looking back matters is covered in the article on reading faster.
learn_rsvp_holds_rubin: Reading words in RSVP can be very fast. Rubin and Turano (1992) had 13 readers read short passages aloud at 1171 words per minute in RSVP, against 303 on a page. In silent reading, 6 of them reached the fastest rate tested, 1652 words per minute, with at least 75% on comprehension.
learn_rsvp_holds_rubin_caveat: The passages were short and 75% is a lenient threshold. This measures word recognition, not the understanding you need to study a text.
learn_rsvp_holds_oquist: On a small screen with short texts, RSVP was 33% faster with no loss of comprehension or extra task load (Öquist and Goldstein, 2003; 16 participants).
learn_rsvp_holds_adaptive: Adaptive RSVP, which varies the timing, lowered task load compared with fixed RSVP in the same work.
learn_rsvp_holds_adhd: Moussaoui, Siddiqi, Cheung and Niemeier (2025) tested 38 students with ADHD and 38 without. At about 200 words per minute, readers with ADHD scored about 7% better with RSVP than in the conditions where the eyes move. Readers without ADHD scored about 6% worse, a trend that was not statistically significant. The authors call their work an “initial step”.
learn_rsvp_holds_adhd_more: Its limits are set out on the ADHD reading tool page.
learn_rsvp_costs_spritz: Benedetto and colleagues (2015) tested Spritz, which shows words with RSVP and lines each one up on a recognition point. Compared with normal reading, it impaired literal comprehension and increased visual fatigue. Fewer blinks is the suggested cause of the fatigue. They blame the loss of comprehension on the absence of a preview of the next word and of look-backs.
learn_rsvp_costs_reply: Ricciardi and Di Nocera (2017) replied with two experiments of 172 participants in all. Comprehension fell once the RSVP speed went above normal reading speed, about 250 words per minute.
learn_rsvp_costs_long: Öquist and Goldstein (2003) also tested long texts. Reading speed and comprehension stayed the same, but task load rose significantly.
learn_rsvp_costs_rates: How fast RSVP can go depends on the method: published rates range from 100 to 1500 words per minute (Primativo et al., 2016). In that work eye movements cost about 250 words per minute, and the authors infer a practical “speed limit of 300 WPM” for normal reading. Comprehension was not measured.
learn_rsvp_orp_title: Lining words up on a letter.
learn_rsvp_orp_ovp: A word is recognised fastest when the eye first lands slightly left of its centre. This is the Optimal Viewing Position effect (O'Regan and Jacobs, 1992).
learn_rsvp_orp_speeedy: Speeedy lines each word up on a letter slightly left of its centre, the ORP, and marks that letter in red.
learn_rsvp_orp_saccades: Eye-movement research puts the time spent moving the eyes (saccades) at roughly 10% of reading time, with fixations taking the rest (Rayner, 1998).
learn_rsvp_orp_untested: Nobody has shown that lining words up this way improves comprehension in RSVP. The only controlled study of Spritz found that the package as a whole hurt comprehension (Benedetto et al., 2015).
learn_rsvp_use_summary: Taken together, the work above points one way: near a reader's normal speed, RSVP on short texts came out close to page reading, and above it comprehension fell. Treat very high speeds as skimming.
learn_rsvp_use_try: You can try it on your own text and change the speed at any time while you read.
learn_avg_title: Average Reading Speed: 238 WPM for Non-Fiction | Speeedy
learn_avg_description: Adults reading English silently average 238 words per minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction, across 190 studies. Most fall between 175 and 300.
learn_avg_lead: Where the average comes from, the range around it, and what a single number can and cannot tell you.
learn_avg_summary: The adult average, the usual range, and why the numbers you see online differ.
learn_avg_average_figures: Brysbaert (2019) reviewed 190 studies with 18,573 participants. For English adults reading silently, the average is 238 words per minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction.
learn_avg_chart_caption: Silent reading speed of English adults, from Brysbaert (2019): the range most adults fall in for non-fiction, and the averages for non-fiction and fiction. An illustration of the figures in the text.
learn_avg_chart_alt: Chart of silent reading speed in words per minute. Most adults read non-fiction between {low} and {high}. The average is {nonFiction} for non-fiction and {fiction} for fiction.
learn_avg_range_spread: Most adults fall between 175 and 300 words per minute for non-fiction (Brysbaert, 2019).
learn_avg_differ_rates: A reading speed depends on the method used to measure it. Published rates for RSVP alone range from 100 to 1500 words per minute (Primativo et al., 2016).
learn_avg_differ_task: It depends on the task too. Rubin and Turano (1992) had 13 readers read short passages aloud at 1171 words per minute in RSVP, against 303 on a page. That measures word recognition, not study-level understanding.
learn_avg_half_tradeoff: Speed and accuracy trade off (Rayner et al., 2016), so a words-per-minute figure means little without a check on what was understood.
learn_avg_half_more: What the research supports about reading faster is in the article on how to read faster.

privacy_description: What Speeedy collects, where it goes and which companies handle it. Your documents stay on your device unless you turn on a Plus feature, and we ask first.
privacy_lead: What Speeedy collects, where it goes and who handles it.
privacy_short: Speeedy reads your documents on your device. Nothing you read leaves it unless you turn on a Plus feature that needs our servers, and we ask first. No ad trackers, no sale of your data, no account to read.
privacy_controller_before: Speeedy is operated by SamDev LLC, a Delaware company. For anything about your privacy, including a request to delete or export your data, write to
privacy_terms_before: The rules for using Speeedy and Plus are in the
privacy_reading_text: No account, no cookie, no upload. The Library, Positions, Sessions, training results and settings live in your browser's storage on your device. Clearing site data erases them. The Share Link you create carries its text in the link itself. Analytics events are anonymous and described below.
privacy_account_sign_in: One verified email address, needed for Plus. Sign-in is a 6-digit code sent to that address. The session is one cookie, HttpOnly, lasting a year from last use; it's the only cookie Speeedy sets.
privacy_account_collected: We collect the email, when the Account was created, when it last signed in, the kind of device signed in (browser, installed app, Android app), and Plus status and history. Sessions you sync show what times of day you read.
privacy_sync_text: Off until you turn it on. When on, it stores the documents' text on our servers in the EU (title, text, language, your place in it), your reading preferences and your reading history. Original files never upload. Synced text is encrypted on disk but not end-to-end, so Speeedy could technically read it; we only use it to run Sync. Any document can be kept on this device only, and Sync holds up to {sync} of text. Turning Sync off deletes the server copy at once. Changes are removed from backups within 30 days.
privacy_sync_consent_intro: The consent screen, once per Account:
privacy_sync_consent_lead: Your Library, your place in each document and your reading history stay the same on every device you sign in on.
privacy_sync_consent_stored: The text of synced documents is stored on Speeedy's servers in the EU. It's encrypted on disk but not end-to-end, so Speeedy could technically read it. We only use it for Sync.
privacy_sync_consent_files: Your original files never leave this device.
privacy_sync_consent_history: Your reading history shows what times of day you read.
privacy_sync_consent_device: Any document can be kept on this device only. Sync holds up to {sync} of text.
privacy_sync_consent_off: Turn Sync off whenever you like on your account page, and the server copy is deleted.
privacy_voices_text: Reading text aloud with a server voice sends the text of the sentences being spoken to our voice server (Modal, in the EU), which returns audio. The text isn't kept there after the request, and the audio is cached on your device. Picking a server voice for the first time shows this once:
privacy_voices_consent_text: The sentences you listen to are sent to our voice server in the EU to be turned into speech. Nothing is kept after the audio is made, and the audio is saved on this device.
privacy_voices_not_now: "Not now" leaves Listen working with the voices on your device.
privacy_analytics_lead: No cookies, unless you sign in to Plus. No ad trackers. Anonymous usage events and crash reports, sent through our server to PostHog, without your IP address.
privacy_analytics_events_link: See the full list of events
privacy_analytics_visit: Each Visit gets a random ID that exists only in memory and is gone on reload; events are a fixed list of counts and choices, never document text, and PostHog is not allowed to build a profile of a reader. Crash reports carry the file, line and function where the error happened, and no messages, no variables and no document text. The extension sends nothing.
privacy_analytics_feedback: Feedback and survey answers go the same way: through our server to PostHog, without your IP address and with no field for your email address. They include whatever you type into the form.
privacy_newsletter_text: If you subscribe, your email and chosen topics are stored by Buttondown in the US. You confirm by email before anything is sent. Every issue has a one-click unsubscribe link. No tracking pixels, no tracked links.
privacy_newsletter_erase: Buttondown keeps the address on its suppression list after unsubscribing; asking us to erase it removes that too.
privacy_payments_text: Plus is sold by Polar, which acts as merchant of record: it takes your payment and handles tax, under its own privacy policy. Speeedy receives your email address, your Plus status and your invoices' totals, never your card details.
privacy_payments_cookies: Polar and Stripe set their own cookies on the checkout page; Speeedy sets none. When Plus ends or an Account is deleted, the provider keeps the payment records tax law requires.
privacy_proc_intro: One row for each company: why we use it, what it handles and where.
privacy_proc_cloudflare_data: For an Account: the Account itself, its Sessions, Positions and settings, Plus status and the markers for deleted documents (database); synced document text (storage); and the sign-in emails.
privacy_proc_cloudflare_where: Database and storage in the EU.
privacy_proc_modal_data: The text of the sentences a server voice speaks. It isn't kept after the request.
privacy_proc_posthog_why: Analytics, crash reports, feedback and surveys
privacy_proc_posthog_data: Anonymous usage events and crash reports, feedback and survey answers. No IP address, no Account ID and no person profile.

privacy_extension_text: The Speeedy extension sends the page you are on to a Speeedy tab in the same browser. It has no server of its own and no sign-in, and it collects nothing. Its Firefox data declaration is set to none.
privacy_extension_tab: The page text goes to a tab in your own browser, not off your device. What that tab does is covered by this policy.
privacy_extension_local: The title and address of the page you send are kept only on your device, in your Library.

terms_pledge_text: Everything that runs on your device is free forever, there are no ads ever, and no account is needed to read. Cutting a feature is allowed; putting one behind payment is not.
terms_pledge_outside: The Free Pledge and the consent rule sit outside the clause that lets these Terms change.
terms_consent_text: No feature that sends your text to Speeedy's servers is ever on by default, and each asks before it starts.
terms_reading_text: Your documents stay yours. We claim no licence over them beyond what it takes to run a feature you turned on, and that ends when you turn it off.
terms_plus_price: Plus costs {annual} a year or {monthly} a month, with a {launch} first-year offer until 30 days after announce day. It renews automatically until cancelled.
terms_plus_cancel: Cancel any time through the provider's portal and Plus runs to the end of the paid period.
terms_plus_refund: Refunds: a full refund on request within 14 days of your first purchase, which also covers the EU 14-day right of withdrawal. After that, cancel and keep the time you paid for.
terms_plus_voices: Server voices are capped at {hours} hours a month.
terms_plus_change: A price change applies from your next renewal and never to time you already paid for.
terms_servers_text: Plus needs an internet connection and depends on Cloudflare, Modal and Polar. When the API is down, the reader keeps working on what's on the device.
terms_accounts_text: An Account is for one person and must use an email you control. Plus is for adults: 18 or over, ticked when the Account is created. The free app has no age limit, because it collects nothing about you.
terms_changes_text: We email every Plus Account at least 30 days before a change to price, features or these Terms affects them. The newsletter may repeat it and is never the only notice.
terms_ending_text: If Plus is ever shut down, every subscriber gets 30 days' email notice, a refund of unused paid annual time, and an export of everything on our servers. Device features keep working, which is the Free Pledge.
terms_rules_use: Acceptable use: don't use Speeedy to break the law or someone else's rights.
terms_rules_warranty: No warranty beyond what the law requires: the app is provided as is, and we're not liable for what you read with it.
terms_rules_consumer: Consumer rights: the law of your own country may give you rights these Terms can't take away.
terms_law_text: Delaware, USA, with the mandatory consumer protections of the reader's home country kept.
